description: Checks whether a candidate can schedule, write, file, supply and protect information in a busy office.

competencies.name: Scheduling & Coordination
competencies.description: Managing diaries, appointments, visitors and meetings so that work runs smoothly.

competencies.name: Business Correspondence
competencies.description: Writing and sending clear, correct and polite letters, emails and notices.

competencies.name: Filing & Information Handling
competencies.description: Filing, tracking and retrieving documents so that they can be found quickly.

competencies.name: Office Operations & Supplies
competencies.description: Controlling stationery, petty cash and equipment in the office.

competencies.name: Confidentiality & Professional Conduct
competencies.description: Protecting sensitive information and behaving professionally with staff and visitors.

questions.text: Which is the best way to avoid double-booking an executive's appointments?

options.text: Remember the appointments and tell the executive each morning
Write each appointment on a separate piece of paper and keep them all in a desk drawer until needed
Keep one shared diary or calendar and update it every time an appointment is made
Let each visitor choose any time and note it later

questions.explanation: A single, up-to-date diary shows all commitments in one place, so clashes are seen before they happen.

questions.text: Your manager has a meeting at 10:00. At 9:50 a visitor with no appointment says his matter is urgent. What should you do first?

options.text: Ask him to wait without telling the manager he has arrived
Ask politely what the matter is, check with the manager, and offer a short slot or take a message
Tell him the manager is busy in meetings all day and that he must make an appointment for next week
Send him straight into the manager's office because he says it is urgent

questions.explanation: A good assistant finds out the purpose, lets the manager decide, and offers a practical alternative without being rude.

questions.text: You are organising a staff meeting. Which of the following should you do? Select all that apply.

options.text: Record minutes that show decisions, action points and who is responsible
Send a notice with the date, time, venue and agenda in good time
Send the notice on the morning of the meeting so people cannot refuse
Leave out the agenda so that discussion stays flexible
Confirm that the venue and any equipment are ready

questions.explanation: Advance notice with an agenda, a ready venue and minutes with action owners make a meeting productive.

questions.text: You begin a formal letter with "Dear Sir/Madam" because you do not know the name. How should you close it?

options.text: Best wishes always
Yours sincerely
Your friend
Yours faithfully

questions.explanation: In formal British-style letters, "Dear Sir/Madam" is closed with "Yours faithfully"; "Yours sincerely" is for a named person.

questions.text: Your manager asks you to email a supplier a quotation. The draft is ready. What should you check before pressing Send?

options.text: Nothing, because any mistake can be corrected in a later email
That the message is marked high importance so it is read first
The recipient address, the attachment, the amounts and the spelling
That many senior staff are copied, so the supplier takes it seriously

questions.explanation: Checking address, attachment and figures prevents errors that can cost money or damage the school's reputation.

questions.text: Which actions make a business email professional? Select all that apply.

options.text: Writing a clear subject line that states the topic
Stating the request and the deadline in simple, polite words
Using capital letters to show the important parts
Using short text-message spellings to save the reader's time
Reading the message again to correct mistakes before sending

questions.explanation: A clear subject, a polite and specific request, and careful proofreading are marks of professional writing.

questions.text: Which approach helps staff find letters and files quickly?

options.text: Keep new letters in a pile and file them at the end of the term
Let every staff member file documents in the way he or she personally finds easiest and quickest
Use one agreed filing system, such as numbered subject files, with an index
File by the colour of the paper the letter is written on

questions.explanation: One agreed system with an index means anyone can file and retrieve documents in the same way.

questions.text: The head teacher needs a file urgently, but it is not in the cabinet. What is the best first step?

options.text: Check the file movement register to see who took it and contact that person
Tell the head teacher the file has been lost and cannot be found
Open every other file in the cabinet and search through the papers
Ask the head teacher to remember the contents and write them again

questions.explanation: A movement (file-out) record shows who holds the file, so it can be traced quickly.

questions.text: The office has old files and a cabinet that is full. What must be done before any file is destroyed?

options.text: Check the retention rules, get approval from the responsible officer, and record what was destroyed
Move them to a store room and forget about them
Ask the cleaner to remove the oldest files from the cabinet whenever there is no more space for new ones
Remove files that have not been opened for one term and burn them

questions.explanation: Records may only be destroyed after the retention period has been checked and approval given, with a record of the disposal.

questions.text: What is the best way to avoid running out of stationery such as paper and pens?

options.text: Wait until staff complain, then buy what is missing
Allow each staff member to keep their own supply in a drawer
Keep a stock register and reorder when the minimum level is reached
Buy a very large amount once a year and keep it in the head's office

questions.explanation: Recording stock and setting a reorder level shows in advance when to buy, without wasting money or running out.

questions.text: You buy printer toner using petty cash, but the shop gives no receipt. What should you do?

options.text: Write the amount from memory in the petty cash book, because the shop is well known and trusted by the school
Pay it back from your own pocket and say nothing
Ask your manager to sign that the money was spent
Ask the shop for a proper receipt or written invoice, and record the payment on a petty cash voucher

questions.explanation: Every petty cash payment needs supporting evidence so that the spending can be checked later.

questions.text: A caller says he is from a government office and asks for a colleague's home address and salary. You cannot confirm who he is. What do you do?

options.text: Say that you do not know and end the call immediately
Give the address but not the salary, because the address is public information and the salary is private
Politely refuse, take his name and number, and pass the request to your manager or HR
Give both, because a government office has the right to know

questions.explanation: Personal details must not be given to unverified callers; the request should go to someone authorised to decide.

description: Checks whether a candidate can organise, protect, keep, back up and correct student and staff records responsibly.

competencies.name: Filing Systems & Classification
competencies.description: Organising paper and electronic records so they can be found and tracked.

competencies.name: Confidentiality & Data Protection
competencies.description: Allowing access to personal records only to authorised people and for proper reasons.

competencies.name: Retention & Disposal
competencies.description: Knowing how long records are kept and how they are safely disposed of.

competencies.name: Digital Records & Backup
competencies.description: Protecting electronic records with backups, accounts and passwords.

competencies.name: Accuracy & Record Integrity
competencies.description: Keeping records correct and correcting mistakes in a traceable way.

questions.text: A school files each student's folder in order of admission number (0001, 0002, 0003...). What is this filing method called?

options.text: Alphabetical filing
Geographical filing
Chronological filing
Numerical filing

questions.explanation: Arranging folders by number is numerical filing; an index is normally kept to find names.

questions.text: The office needs a student's file for a transfer, but you cannot find it. What should you do first?

options.text: Remove files of other students until you find it
Check the movement register, then look in nearby places and under other spellings of the name
Tell the parent the file is lost and start a new one using the documents the parent can bring again
Ask the student to bring copies of all documents again

questions.explanation: Most "lost" files are signed out or misfiled, so the register and similar spellings are checked before any file is declared lost.

questions.text: Which practices help prevent misfiling? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keeping unlabelled folders to save stationery
Filing documents daily instead of leaving them in a pile
Allowing staff to return folders to any shelf they prefer
Using clear, consistent labels and numbers on every folder
Placing a file-out card in the cabinet when a file is removed

questions.explanation: Consistent labelling, file-out cards and regular filing keep records where they are expected to be.

questions.text: Who should be allowed to see a student's disciplinary record?

options.text: Any teacher who is curious about the student
Visitors who ask politely at the office
Only authorised staff who need it for their work
Any parent at the school

questions.explanation: Access to personal records is limited to people with a genuine work reason and authority.

questions.text: A parent asks to see the results file of her daughter's classmate "to compare". What should you do?

options.text: Politely refuse and explain that you can only share her own child's information
Show only the marks and keep back the other details such as comments, fees and the discipline record
Show it if she promises to keep it private
Show the file because the girls are in the same class

questions.explanation: A student's information may only be shared with the parent or guardian of that student, or other authorised people.

questions.text: A teacher asks you to email the full student register with parents' phone numbers to his personal email so he can work at home. What is the best response?

options.text: Do not send it until it is approved under school policy, and suggest a secure approved way to share it
Send it, because he is a trusted member of staff
Send it with a password on the file, because the password protects it, and tell the head teacher about it later
Send only the phone numbers and remove the names

questions.explanation: Personal data should leave the school systems only with authority and in a secure, approved way.

questions.text: What is a records retention schedule?

options.text: A timetable showing when the records office opens and closes
A list of the cabinets and shelves used to store records
A list showing how long each type of record is kept and what is done with it afterwards
A register of who borrowed each file this term

questions.explanation: A retention schedule sets the keeping period and final action (destroy or archive) for each record type.

questions.text: Records have passed their retention period. Which are correct ways to dispose of them? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recording what was destroyed, when, and who approved it
Placing whole files in a general rubbish bin
Deleting electronic copies, including those on backups, as policy requires
Shredding or burning confidential paper records after approval
Giving the files to staff to take home as scrap paper

questions.explanation: Disposal must be approved, complete, secure and documented so that confidential data cannot be read afterwards.

questions.text: What is a backup?

options.text: The older version of a file that was deleted by mistake
A copy of files kept in a separate place so they can be restored if the originals are lost
A password that protects the file from other users who try to open or copy it without permission
A second name given to an important file on the same computer

questions.explanation: A backup is a separate copy, so loss or damage of the original does not mean loss of the data.

questions.text: All student records are kept on one office computer, and the only backup is a flash disk kept in the same drawer. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Make a backup once every year during the holidays
Stop using the computer for student records and keep everything on paper files in a locked cabinet in the main office
Make regular backups kept in a different secure place, such as off-site or in cloud storage, and test them
Buy a second flash disk and keep it in the same drawer

questions.explanation: A backup stored beside the computer is lost in the same fire or theft; copies must be separate, regular and tested.

questions.text: Which arrangement best protects a student records system?

options.text: No passwords, but the office door is locked
One shared password written on the wall for all clerks
One administrator account used by everyone for speed
Each user has a personal account and password, with access matching his or her job

questions.explanation: Personal accounts and role-based access make users accountable and limit who can see or change records.

questions.text: A student's date of birth in the admission register is different from the one on the birth certificate. What should you do?

options.text: Cover the old date with correction fluid and rewrite it
Verify with the certificate, get approval, and correct the record following procedure with a note of the change
Change the register quietly so it matches the certificate
Leave it as it is, because the admission register was filled in first and is regarded as the official record of the school

questions.explanation: Corrections must be verified, authorised and traceable, never hidden, so that the record stays reliable.

description: Checks whether a candidate can run the daily school office: admissions, registers, timetables, official requirements and parent contact.

competencies.name: Admissions & Student Records
competencies.description: Admitting and transferring pupils with correct documents and records.

competencies.name: Attendance & Timetabling
competencies.description: Keeping attendance registers and arranging timetables and cover for absent teachers.

competencies.name: Compliance & Reporting
competencies.description: Meeting ministry, regional and NECTA requirements accurately and on time.

competencies.name: Parent & Stakeholder Communication
competencies.description: Communicating clearly and respectfully with parents and guardians.

competencies.name: Child Safety & School Procedures
competencies.description: Following safe procedures for pupil pick-up, visitors, accidents and incidents.

questions.text: Which document best proves a new pupil's date of birth at admission?

options.text: The birth certificate or an equivalent official document
The parent's phone number and address
The class list of the previous school
The receipt for the first school fees payment

questions.explanation: Official proof of age protects the pupil and avoids errors later, for example in examination registration.

questions.text: A parent comes in the middle of the term to transfer her child but has no transfer letter or report from the old school. What should you do?

options.text: Explain the required documents and ask the previous school for the release letter and records before admitting
Refuse admission completely and tell her that the school does not take pupils who change schools during the term
Ask the child to say which class he was in and admit him
Admit the child at once and never ask for any records

questions.explanation: Transfers need the child's records to be requested and verified so the correct class and history are known.

questions.text: Why must daily class attendance registers be filled in accurately?

options.text: They are official records used to follow up absent pupils and to support reports
They are used only to calculate fee balances
They are used only to decide the teachers' salaries
They are needed only to prove attendance to the examination board during the NECTA examinations

questions.explanation: Attendance registers are official records that show who was present and help the school act on absences.

questions.text: Which should be considered when preparing the school timetable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving each teacher any periods he or she requests, regardless of workload
The number of periods the syllabus requires for each subject
The availability of classrooms and laboratories
Putting all practical subjects on one day to save effort
That no teacher or class is placed in two lessons at the same time

questions.explanation: A workable timetable meets syllabus time, avoids clashes and fits the rooms and teachers available.

questions.text: On Monday morning a teacher is absent without notice and Form 3 has no teacher for period 2. What is the best action?

options.text: Let the students go out until the next period starts
Ask the class monitor to teach the lesson alone
Use the cover arrangement to assign an available teacher, inform the head, and record the absence
Combine all classes in the hall with no teacher

questions.explanation: A cover arrangement keeps pupils supervised and learning, and the absence is recorded for follow-up.

questions.text: Which body prepares and administers national examinations such as PSLE and the Form Four examination in Tanzania?

options.text: The Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA)
The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA)
The Tanzania Bureau of Standards (TBS)
The National Examinations Council of Tanzania (NECTA)

questions.explanation: NECTA is responsible for national examinations, and schools register their candidates with it.

questions.text: Four weeks before the exams you find that a candidate's name in the NECTA registration list is spelt differently from his birth certificate. What should you do?

options.text: Wait until after the results and then ask for a new certificate
Tell the pupil to use the spelling on the list from now on, since the list has already been submitted to NECTA and cannot be changed
Change the school's records to match the list and say nothing
Report to the head immediately and follow NECTA's procedure for correcting candidate details, with supporting documents

questions.explanation: Candidate details must be corrected through the official process before the exam so that results and certificates are correct.

questions.text: School quality assurance officers will visit the school. Which records should the office have ready? Select all that apply.

options.text: Private bank statements of the teachers
Attendance registers for all classes
The head teacher's personal diary and letters
Staff files showing qualifications and appointments
The admission register and pupil enrolment records

questions.explanation: Officers check school records such as admission, attendance and staff files; private documents are not part of school records.

questions.text: An angry parent says the fee statement shows a wrong balance. What is the best way to respond?

options.text: Ask him to come back when the accountant is not busy
Listen calmly, check the records with the accounts office, explain the result, and follow up
Promise to reduce the balance so he calms down
Tell him the computer is always correct, the statement cannot be wrong, and he must pay before the end of the week

questions.explanation: Listening, checking facts and giving a clear answer settles disputes and keeps the parent's trust.

questions.text: The school has a new closing date for the term. How should parents be informed?

options.text: By telling only the parents who visit the office
By posting the date on the staff notice board only
By an official written notice or SMS sent to all parents, with a copy kept
By telling pupils to remember it and tell their parents

questions.explanation: Official channels reach all parents and leave a record of what was communicated.

questions.text: During school hours a man says he is a pupil's uncle and wants to take the child home. The pupil's file does not list him. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the child if he knows the man, and release him if yes
Let the man wait in the classroom with the child
Release the child because the man knows the pupil's full name and says that the parents have sent him
Do not release the pupil; verify with the parent or guardian and inform the head teacher

questions.explanation: Pupils are released only to people authorised by their parent or guardian, after identity is checked.

questions.text: A pupil is hurt while playing and is given first aid. What should the school office do after this?

options.text: Record nothing about it, because the pupil is now feeling better and has returned to class to continue the lessons
Record the incident only if the parent complains
Tell the parent only if the pupil asks you to
Record the incident, the action taken and the time in the incident book, and inform the parent

questions.explanation: Incidents are recorded and parents informed so the school is accountable and the child receives proper follow-up.

description: Checks whether a candidate can classify, catalogue, lend, care for and account for a school library collection.

competencies.name: Classification & Cataloguing
competencies.description: Classifying books by Dewey Decimal Classification and describing them in catalogue records.

competencies.name: Circulation & Lending
competencies.description: Issuing, returning and following up borrowed items fairly and accurately.

competencies.name: Collection Care & Stock Management
competencies.description: Protecting books from damage and managing the collection by weeding and stock checks.

competencies.name: Reading Promotion & User Services
competencies.description: Encouraging pupils to read and helping users find what they need.

competencies.name: Library Records & Policies
competencies.description: Keeping accession registers, stock records and written library rules.

questions.text: In the Dewey Decimal Classification, which main class covers natural sciences and mathematics?
questions.explanation: The 500 class contains natural sciences and mathematics (for example mathematics 510, physics 530, chemistry 540).

questions.text: A Form Two Chemistry textbook arrives at the library. Under Dewey, which number is the best fit?
questions.explanation: Chemistry is classified at 540; 510 is mathematics, 570 is life sciences and 630 is agriculture.

questions.text: A new book discusses "the chemistry of soils for maize farming". You are unsure of the class. What is the correct rule?

options.text: Classify it by the main subject the book treats most fully, and note other subjects in the catalogue
Classify it under the subject the borrower is likely to ask for
Place it where the shelf has the most free space
Classify it under whichever subject comes first alphabetically in the list of Dewey class names and headings

questions.explanation: Books are classified by their predominant subject, not by convenience or alphabetical order.

questions.text: Which details normally appear in a catalogue record of a book? Select all that apply.

options.text: The name of the pupil who borrowed it last
The name of the teacher who placed it on the shelf
Author and title
Class number or call number
Publisher, place and year of publication

questions.explanation: A catalogue record describes the item itself: who wrote it, who published it and where it is classified.

questions.text: What is the purpose of an accession number?

options.text: It identifies each individual copy, in the order it was added to the library
It is the same for all copies of the same title
It shows the subject that the book is about
It shows the pupil who borrowed the book

questions.explanation: Each physical copy receives its own accession number, recorded in the accession register.

questions.text: A pupil wants to take the reference dictionary home, but reference books are for use in the library only. What should you do?

options.text: Lend it for one night only, because he promises to return it first thing the next morning before lessons
Lend it only if he is a prefect or a friend of the librarian
Explain the rule, let him use it in the library, and offer another suitable book to borrow
Refuse and tell him to stop asking for reference books

questions.explanation: The rule protects reference books for all users; the librarian stays helpful by offering alternatives.

questions.text: A pupil returns a book two weeks late. The library rules include a penalty for late returns. How should you apply the rule?

options.text: Apply the written rule in the same way to every borrower
Ignore it because the book was returned in good condition
Charge double so that others learn from the example
Waive it for pupils who are in your class or friendly with you

questions.explanation: Fair and consistent application of written rules maintains trust and discipline in the library.

questions.text: A pupil insists he returned a book, but the records show it is still on loan. What is the best response?

options.text: Tell him to bring a replacement copy first
Remove the loan from the record straight away to avoid an argument and keep the library quiet and calm for others
Accuse him of lying and charge him for the book immediately
Check the shelves and return trays and the records for errors, and stay polite while you investigate

questions.explanation: Records and shelves can contain mistakes, so facts are checked calmly before any charge is made.

questions.text: Which practices help to preserve library books? Select all that apply.

options.text: Not allowing food and drink near the books
Keeping the library dry and well ventilated
Shelving books upright without overcrowding the shelf
Leaving books in direct sunlight to prevent mould
Repairing torn pages with ordinary sticky tape

questions.explanation: Dry, ventilated and clean conditions protect paper; ordinary sticky tape and strong sunlight both damage books.

questions.text: What does "weeding" a library collection mean?

options.text: Moving the books to other classrooms to share
Removing items that are damaged, out of date or no longer useful, according to a policy
Adding new books that were donated by parents
Cleaning the shelves and dusting the books every week so that they stay in good condition for all the pupils

questions.explanation: Weeding removes unsuitable items so the collection stays accurate, useful and easy to use.

questions.text: Few pupils visit the library. Which action is most likely to increase reading?

options.text: Make the rules stricter and increase the fines on late books
Keep the library locked outside lesson hours and allow only teachers to borrow so that no books are lost
Start reading clubs, display new books and set a reading period in the timetable
Buy only textbooks used in examinations

questions.explanation: Active promotion, attractive displays and a regular time to read build a reading habit.

questions.text: At the end of the year you do a stocktake. How is it normally done?

options.text: Count only the books that were borrowed this year
Count the number of shelves and multiply by the books per shelf
Compare the books on the shelves with the accession register and record missing items
Ask pupils and teachers which books they think are missing and write down the titles they mention

questions.explanation: Checking the shelf against the accession register shows exactly which copies are missing, and losses can then be reported.

description: Checks whether a candidate can manage contracts, leave, discipline, appraisal and staff records fairly and lawfully.

competencies.name: Employment Contracts & Records
competencies.description: Preparing written contracts and keeping confidential, accurate staff files.

competencies.name: Leave & Attendance
competencies.description: Managing leave and absence fairly and in line with policy.

competencies.name: Discipline & Grievance
competencies.description: Handling misconduct and complaints with fair procedure and documentation.

competencies.name: Performance Appraisal
competencies.description: Running fair, evidence-based performance appraisals and improvement plans.

competencies.name: Labour Law Basics
competencies.description: Understanding basic principles of fair termination and labour dispute handling in Tanzania.

questions.text: Why should every employee have a written employment contract?

options.text: It is needed only when the employee is a foreigner
It is needed only for the head of the organisation
It allows the employer to change the terms at any time without discussing the changes with the employee
It records agreed terms such as duties, pay, hours and leave, so both sides know their obligations

questions.explanation: A written contract avoids misunderstandings by recording the terms both parties have agreed.

questions.text: A new teacher will start on Monday, but his contract is not ready. The manager says to "sort it out later". What is the best action?

options.text: Let him start and sign the contract only when a problem appears
Tell him that a verbal promise is enough for a teacher and that the written contract will be prepared in due course
Ask him to write his own contract and sign it
Prepare the contract so that it is explained and signed at or before the start date, and keep a copy

questions.explanation: Terms should be in writing at the start, explained to the employee and signed, with copies kept.

questions.text: Which information should a written employment contract normally include? Select all that apply.

options.text: The income of the employee's spouse
Job title and main duties
The employee's private medical history
Salary and how and when it is paid
Working hours and leave arrangements

questions.explanation: A contract states the job, pay and working conditions; private matters unrelated to the job do not belong in it.

questions.text: How should personnel files containing salaries, warnings and personal details be kept?

options.text: In the head's car so that they are always available
In a locked cabinet or protected system, accessible only to authorised HR staff
In a shared folder that every employee can open
On an open shelf in the staff room so that managers and heads of departments can see them easily

questions.explanation: Personnel files hold sensitive information and must be kept confidential and secure.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of keeping leave records for each employee?

options.text: To punish employees who take leave
To track leave entitlement, leave taken and leave balance
To show visitors how many employees the school has
To decide which employees to promote

questions.explanation: Leave records show what each employee is entitled to, has taken and still has left.

questions.text: A teacher asks for annual leave in the middle of exam week, when staffing is tight. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain the operational problem, agree alternative dates in line with policy, and record the decision in writing
Approve it verbally and leave the class uncovered
Refuse without any discussion, tell her not to ask again this year, and note the request as a disciplinary problem
Tell her that she has no right to leave at all

questions.explanation: Employers may agree dates with the employee based on business needs, but must discuss it fairly and record the outcome.

questions.text: An employee is often late. His supervisor wants to dismiss him immediately without telling him. What should HR advise?

options.text: Agree, because repeated lateness is misconduct that gives the employer the right to dismiss him at once without any process
Reduce his salary without telling him
Ignore the lateness so that the problem goes away
Follow a fair process: discuss the problem, give documented warnings, and allow him to respond before any decision

questions.explanation: Fair procedure means the employee knows the concern, gets warnings and a chance to respond.

questions.text: A serious misconduct case is being handled. Which steps are part of a fair disciplinary process? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving him a chance to respond, with the outcome recorded in writing
Telling the employee clearly what he is accused of
Deciding the outcome before the hearing to save time
Announcing the case in a staff meeting before the hearing
Investigating the facts before deciding

questions.explanation: A fair process includes investigation, notice of the allegation, a hearing and a written outcome, handled with confidentiality.

questions.text: A female employee tells you in private that her supervisor harasses her. She asks you to keep it confidential. What is the best first step?

options.text: Take her seriously, record her complaint in writing, and arrange an impartial investigation with limited disclosure
Tell her to ignore it and wait to see whether it happens again
Confront the supervisor in front of the other staff, name the employee who complained, and demand an explanation at once
Share the story with colleagues to find out whether it is true

questions.explanation: Complaints of harassment must be taken seriously, recorded and investigated fairly, with confidentiality respected as far as possible.

questions.text: Which feature makes a performance appraisal fair?

options.text: It is based on the supervisor's memory of the last week
It uses agreed objectives, evidence of results and regular feedback
It is used only when the employer wants to dismiss someone
It compares the employees' personal characters rather than their work

questions.explanation: Fair appraisal is based on agreed, measurable expectations and documented evidence.

questions.text: An appraisal shows that a teacher's performance is below standard. What should the manager do next?

options.text: Discuss the results openly, agree clear improvement targets with support, and set a review date
Wait until the next year to mention it
Place the report in the personnel file without telling the teacher, and use it later if there is a problem
Tell other teachers about the poor result

questions.explanation: Employees must be told about performance problems and given a fair chance to improve with support and a review.

questions.text: An employee believes his dismissal was unfair and the matter is not settled at the workplace. Which body usually deals with the dispute first?

options.text: The Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA)
The National Examinations Council of Tanzania (NECTA)
The Commission for Mediation and Arbitration (CMA)
The Tanzania Bureau of Standards (TBS)

questions.explanation: Under Tanzania's labour laws, labour disputes are referred first to the CMA for mediation and arbitration.

description: Checks whether a candidate can define a job, advertise it, shortlist and interview fairly, verify candidates and welcome new staff.

competencies.name: Job Analysis & Advertising
competencies.description: Defining the job and the person needed and advertising openly.

competencies.name: Shortlisting
competencies.description: Selecting candidates for interview using clear and consistent criteria.

competencies.name: Structured Interviewing
competencies.description: Running interviews that are consistent, job-related and free of discrimination.

competencies.name: Reference & Background Checks
competencies.description: Verifying qualifications, experience and conduct before making an offer.

competencies.name: Fair Hiring & Onboarding
competencies.description: Avoiding bias and conflicts of interest and welcoming new employees properly.

questions.text: Which document sets out the qualifications, skills and experience a successful candidate must have?

options.text: The leave register
The offer letter
The employee's payslip
The person specification

questions.explanation: The person specification describes the person needed; the job description describes the job itself.

questions.text: Which details should a good job advertisement contain? Select all that apply.

options.text: The essential qualifications and experience
The job title and main duties
The name of the person the employer prefers to hire
How and by when to apply
A preferred tribe or religion for applicants

questions.explanation: An advertisement should be clear and open and give all information needed to apply, without discriminating.

questions.text: A teaching post must be filled quickly. The manager wants to tell only his relatives about it. What should you advise?

options.text: Wait until someone visits the office and asks for a job
Advertise only inside the school to avoid costs, so that staff can recommend people they already know
Advertise openly on notice boards and suitable media so that all qualified people can apply
Agree, because relatives are more trustworthy and faster to hire

questions.explanation: Open advertising gives all qualified people a chance and attracts the best candidates.

questions.text: What is the best basis for shortlisting applicants?

options.text: Choose the applicants with the longest letters
Choose the applicants known to the panel
Compare each application against the same essential and desirable criteria
Choose the applicants who live closest to the school

questions.explanation: Using the same job-related criteria for everyone makes shortlisting fair and defensible.

questions.text: You received 80 applications for one position and can interview only six candidates. How should you proceed?

options.text: Score every application against agreed criteria and record the scores to support the shortlist
Read the first ten and interview the best from those
Draw six names without reading the applications
Pick the six whose names you recognise from the community, because they are easier to contact and to trust

questions.explanation: Scoring all applications against agreed criteria gives a fair, recorded shortlist.

questions.text: What is a structured interview?

options.text: Every candidate is asked the same prepared questions and scored against agreed criteria
An interview where each candidate is asked different questions
An interview where the panel has no questions prepared in advance and follows the conversation freely
An interview held in a formal office with a long table

questions.explanation: Using the same prepared questions and scoring makes candidates comparable and the decision fairer.

questions.text: During an interview, a panel member asks a female candidate whether she plans to have children soon. What should you do?

options.text: Politely intervene, explain that the question is not job-related, and return to job-related questions
Say nothing, because it may help the school to plan if it knows her family plans before it makes an offer
Let the candidate answer and note her reply for scoring
End the interview and reject her application

questions.explanation: Questions about pregnancy or family plans are discriminatory and unrelated to ability, so the panel should avoid them.

questions.text: Which are good practices for an interview panel? Select all that apply.

options.text: Take notes during each interview
Score each candidate independently straight after the interview
Ask each candidate whichever questions come to mind
Discuss each candidate with other panel members between interviews and decide early
Agree the questions and the scoring guide before the interviews

questions.explanation: Prepared questions, notes and independent scoring reduce bias and give evidence for the decision.

questions.text: Before contacting a candidate's current employer for a reference, what should you do?

options.text: Contact them secretly without telling the candidate, so that the candidate cannot prepare any answers in advance
Ask the candidate's friends and relatives instead
Contact the employer only after the offer has been accepted
Get the candidate's consent to approach that employer

questions.explanation: A candidate's current job can be put at risk, so consent should be obtained before contacting the employer.

questions.text: A candidate's academic certificate looks altered. What is the proper step?

options.text: Verify the certificate with the awarding body, and do not make the offer until it is confirmed
Ask the candidate to bring a photocopy of the same certificate
Reject the candidate at once and tell other schools
Accept it if the candidate speaks confidently at the interview and has strong experience in the field

questions.explanation: Doubtful documents must be checked with the issuer before a decision is made, without assuming guilt.

questions.text: You discover that a panel member's cousin is one of the applicants. What should happen?

options.text: The panel member declares the relationship and takes no part in assessing that applicant
The panel member gives the cousin lower marks to avoid doubt
Nothing, because a relative can be trusted to be fair
The panel member scores the cousin last so it looks fair

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest must be declared and the person should withdraw from assessing the related applicant.

questions.text: Which action is the best part of onboarding a new employee on his first day?

options.text: Give him the contract only after the first month
Introduce him only to the head of the school
Give the contract and job description, explain key policies, and introduce him to the team and a mentor
Give him a desk and expect him to learn the job on his own by watching how the other employees work each day

questions.explanation: A planned induction helps new staff understand their role and the school's rules and settle in faster.
